paras: The Madison Square mob attack on William Jackson took place on the night of August 9, 1900, when a crowd at a band concert in Madison Square Park, New York City, surrounded a Black man just arrested by police and cried "Lynch him!" Police held off the crowd with nightsticks and took Jackson to the station, where he was charged with disorderly conduct. The story ran outside New York as a threatened lynching, headed "Negro Threatened With Lynching" in the Richmond Times.

A concert by the Twelfth Regiment Band had drawn several thousand people to the square, one of the largest crowds of the year. According to the Tribune, a man told Policeman Eugene O'Sullivan that three "colored men" were "ogling white women"; the Sun said the three had insulted women and seized their arms.

When the policemen approached, the three men ran, and O'Sullivan chased one of them under the Dewey Arch and through the crowd as he dodged among the benches. Once he was caught near the fountain, several hundred men who had joined the pursuit surrounded the policeman and his prisoner, some crying "Lynch him!" The Sun gave the cry as "lynch him: he insulted a girl," while the Tribune said someone had spread a story that he had assaulted a white child.

O'Sullivan knocked several men down with his nightstick, but men in the crowd struck the prisoner's face and drew blood, according to the Tribune; the Sun said he was "kicked and rapped a dozen times." Other patrolmen came to O'Sullivan's aid and took the prisoner to the West Thirtieth Street station, followed by hundreds of people, some still shouting for a lynching.

The prisoner gave his name as William Jackson, a twenty-year-old porter of 225 West Eighteenth Street, and was locked up as a disorderly person. No arrests of crowd members are reported, and no court disposition of Jackson's case appears in the coverage.

Two Manhattan dailies covered the attack the next morning in different terms. The Tribune headlined "Crowd Attacks Prisoner" and wrote of the "mob's fury," noting that the crowd "did not know why the colored man had been chased." The Sun's headline, "Mobbed an Insulting Negro," took the charge as fact, and its story called the chase a "game of tag."

The Sun's text went out on the wire and ran the same day in the Washington Evening Times under "Might Have Been a Lynching," subheaded "Colored Toughs Attacked in New York City." The next day the Richmond Times printed a separate New York letter, headed "Threatened Lynching," in a gossip column between Tammany politics and a street-car robbery.

Accounts differ on whether Jackson was hurt: both New York papers report blows, but the Richmond Times letter said that "no attempt to harm Jackson was made." Estimates of the crowd also vary, from several hundred in the Tribune and 500 in the Sun to "three thousand men and women" in the Richmond Times.

bases: A crowd at a band concert surrounded a Black prisoner in police hands, cried 'Lynch him!' and struck him before police got him away, with no killing reported (A1, A2, A4).

The Tribune, the Sun and a separate New York letter in the Richmond Times agree on the chase, the arrest, the cries of 'Lynch him' and the police escort, though the Richmond Times denies he was harmed (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: Several hundred men surrounded the policeman and prisoner crying 'Lynch him!'; despite nightsticks, men landed blows that cut Jackson's face; the fury came from a rumor that he had assaulted a white child.

accounts.label: The Sun (and its Washington reprint)
accounts.gist: Three Black men insulted women and seized their arms; when someone yelled that Jackson had insulted a girl the crowd joined in, and he was kicked and rapped a dozen times before police dragged him away.

accounts.label: Richmond Times New York letter
accounts.gist: Three thousand people pursued Jackson; the crowd swarmed about him crying 'Lynch him!', but a police circle forced a way to the station and no attempt to harm him was made.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Crowd Attacks Prisoner' and spoke of the 'mob's fury', while repeating the unverified charges and noting the crowd 'did not know why the colored man had been chased'.
The Sun headlined 'Mobbed an Insulting Negro' with the subhead 'Kicks and Cuffs Him Soundly' and treated the chase as a 'game of tag'.
The Washington Evening Times ran the Sun's text as 'Might Have Been a Lynching', subheaded 'Colored Toughs Attacked in New York City'.
The Richmond Times placed the item, headed 'Threatened Lynching', in a New York gossip column between Tammany politics and a street-car robbery.

conflicts.note: The two local New York papers both report blows; the Richmond Times letter alone denies harm. The Tribune's own opening line says nightsticks 'saved the colored man from injury', which its later text qualifies.

versions.value: Several hundred surrounded him and followed
Three thousand men and women pursued him

conflicts.note: The concert crowd was several thousand (A1); the larger figure may count the whole pursuing audience.

versions.value: Ogling white women; rumor in the crowd that he assaulted a white child
Insulting women and seizing their arms; cry that he 'insulted a girl'

conflicts.note: All are accusations relayed by bystanders or reporters; none was tested in the coverage.
